First put your own life in order.

I want to be completely alone right now.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'юрприз'). Common masculine noun meaning 'surprise' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Your surprises are rather strange.
I'll show you one surprise.
What surprise?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'at, near, with', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Ainura, we really should not do this.
What are you talking about?
Now what Senya does—that is theft.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What are you talking about?

examples.text: Ты у меня самый лучший папа.
examples.trans: You are the very best dad.

examples.text: Ты с ней так и не заговорил?
examples.trans: You never actually spoke to her, did you?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'some kind of, some', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What nonsense.
Some man called you.

examples.text: Бред какой-то. Но, с другой стороны, чем я рискую?
examples.trans: What nonsense. But on the other hand, what have I got to lose?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'транный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('strange').

examples.trans: Your surprises are rather strange.
She's really strange.
What a strange man!

meanings.note: Prefix 'под-' ('under, up to') indicates approaching or supporting from below (stem 'ождать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'wait', paired with 'ждать'.

examples.trans: Wait, I'll be right there.
Wait a minute.

examples.text: Подожди, Нин, ты не поняла. Это же стыдно!
examples.trans: Wait, Nina, you don't get it. It's shameful!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Ой, ну и бардак у тебя здесь.
examples.trans: Oh, what a mess you have here.
Is everything going to happen right here today?

examples.text: А ты что, здесь в отеле живёшь?
examples.trans: Do you live here in the hotel?

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Wait right here for literally a minute.
They beat me literally every day!
I understood his words literally.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: After all, this is real theft.
We will take a couple of pieces for the anniversary.

examples.text: Мне тоже казалось, что шеф наблюдает.
examples.trans: It seemed to me too that the chef was watching.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'a minute' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Слушай, ты постой тут пять минут.
examples.trans: Listen, stand right here for five minutes.

examples.text: Мне нужно пять минут, чтобы всё доделать.
examples.trans: I need five minutes to finish everything.

examples.text: Я пошёл, мы будем через пару минут.
examples.trans: I am heading in, we will be there in a couple of minutes.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Этот Спартак даже тут играть не умеет.
examples.trans: This Spartak does not even know how to play here.

examples.text: Подожди, а я тут при чём?
examples.trans: Wait, what do I have to do with this?

examples.text: Шеф, тут не всё так просто.
examples.trans: Chef, not everything is so simple here.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'boyfriend, guy, young man' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Are you my boyfriend?
He is a good guy.
These are my boyfriend's friends.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'with / from', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Ainura, we really should not do this.
After all, this is real theft.
Now what Senya does—that is theft.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'guitar' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: У тебя нет знакомого, который на гитаре играет?
examples.trans: Do you have a friend who plays the guitar?
And does it have to be specifically on the guitar?

examples.text: Да, мне именно гитарист сегодня нужен.
examples.trans: Yes, I specifically need a guitarist today.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Ainura, we really should not do this.
It seems to me someone is over there.

examples.text: Мне тоже казалось, что шеф наблюдает.
examples.trans: It seemed to me too that the chef was watching.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'saw', paired with 'увидеть'.

examples.text: Чтобы я тебя здесь больше не видела!
examples.trans: Let me never see you here again!

examples.text: Ты тут парня с гитарой не видел?
examples.trans: Did you see a guy with a guitar around here?

examples.text: Но ты не можешь запретить видеться с дочкой.
examples.trans: But you cannot forbid me to see our daughter.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'only', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: А ты их только что выкинула.
examples.trans: And you just threw them away.

examples.text: Понятно, значит, он уволит только меня.
examples.trans: I see, so he will fire only me.

examples.text: Тебя может уволить только наш шеф.
examples.trans: Only our chef can fire you.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what, that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What are you talking about?

examples.text: Мне тоже казалось, что шеф наблюдает.
examples.trans: It seemed to me too that the chef was watching.

examples.text: Зато теперь я знаю, что ей нравится.
examples.trans: At least now I know what she likes.

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'сюда').

examples.trans: Do not go anywhere from here.

examples.text: Уходите отсюда и дайте мне поспать!
examples.trans: Get away from here and let me sleep!
He just ran out of here quickly.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Lyova, you need to act faster.
Oguzok, let's work very fast.

examples.text: Вы быстрее кроватку соберёте и уйдёте.
examples.trans: You will assemble the crib faster and leave.

meanings.note: Prefix 'вы-' ('out of') marks outward movement or thorough completion (stem 'бежать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'ran out'.

examples.trans: He just ran out of here quickly.

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и выбежать вовремя.
examples.trans: We need to do everything and ran out on time.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'mom' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Мама, а ты что здесь делаешь?
examples.trans: Mom, what are you doing here?

examples.text: Мама, перестань, не лезь в мою жизнь!
examples.trans: Mom, stop it, stay out of my life!
Mum, where's my phone?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Ainura, we really should not do this.
After all, this is real theft.
What are you talking about?

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'are doing', paired with 'сделать'.

examples.trans: Ainura, we really should not do this.

examples.text: Там ещё полки нужно прибить, сделаешь?
examples.trans: Shelves also need to be put up there, will you do it?

examples.text: А почему он вам предупреждение не сделал?
examples.trans: And why did he not give you a warning?

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'can', paired with 'смочь'.

examples.trans: I can't today.
That can't be.

examples.text: Этого не может быть. Это наша история.
examples.trans: That can't be. It's our history.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to wait, to expect', paired with 'подождать'.

examples.text: Можешь не ждать его, он не вернётся.
examples.trans: You need not wait for him, he will not return.
Don't wait for me.
I'm waiting for you.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'his', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: She is over there all alone right now.

examples.text: Она мужа ни о чём не просит.
examples.trans: She is not asking her husband for anything.

examples.text: Завтра утром моих девчонок выписывают из роддома.
examples.trans: Tomorrow morning my girls are being discharged from the hospital.

meanings.note: Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'will return', paired with 'возвращаться'.

examples.trans: I'll be back soon.
He came back home.

examples.text: Так, не шумим. Я скоро вернусь.
examples.trans: Right, no noise. I'll be back soon.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'why', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Зачем ты наступаешь на те же грабли?
examples.trans: Why do you keep making the exact same mistake?
What have you come for?
What's that for?

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'ступать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to advance, to attack', paired with 'наступить'.

examples.text: Зачем ты наступаешь на те же грабли?
examples.trans: Why do you keep making the exact same mistake?
Enemy troops are advancing!
The army was advancing south.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'those (people)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Этот Спартак даже тут играть не умеет.

examples.text: Давно нужно было выкинуть этот хлам.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'rake (same mistake)' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Зачем ты наступаешь на те же грабли?
examples.trans: Why do you keep making the exact same mistake?

examples.text: На кухне отеля всегда есть грабли.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'after all', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

meanings.en: once, on one occasion, one day
meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'once, one day', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Ведь у вас однажды уже не получилось.
examples.trans: After all, it already failed once for you two.

examples.text: Однажды всё вокруг может резко измениться.
examples.trans: One day everything around can change drastically.

examples.text: Однажды Макс решил стать великим поваром.
examples.trans: One day Max decided to become a great chef.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'already', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Он уже три года добивается меня.
examples.trans: He has been pursuing me for three years already.

examples.text: Да, мне именно гитарист сегодня нужен.
examples.trans: Yes, I specifically need a guitarist today.

examples.text: Да, а ты уже бывал тут?
examples.trans: Yes, have you been here before?

meanings.en: to turn out, to work out
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'лучиться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'turned out', paired with 'получаться'.

examples.text: Мне бы сейчас получить деньги вперёд.
examples.trans: I would like to get the money up front right now.
It will all work out!
He'll make a good doctor.

meanings.note: Prefix 'пере-' denotes crossing over, repeating, or exceeding a limit (stem 'стать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'stop', paired with 'переставать'.

examples.text: Мама, перестань, не лезь в мою жизнь!
examples.trans: Mom, stop it, stay out of my life!

examples.text: Да перестаньте! Я двадцать лет в карты не играла.
examples.trans: Oh, stop it! I haven't played cards for twenty years.
The rain finally stopped.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'poke nose, meddle', paired with 'полезть'.

examples.text: Я сутки из такси не вылезал, людей возил.
examples.trans: I did not get out of my taxi all day, driving people.

examples.text: Мама, перестань, не лезь в мою жизнь!
examples.trans: Mom, stop it, stay out of my life!
Stay out of my life!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Ainura, we really should not do this.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'my', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: This is my present for her.

examples.text: Да, в моём доме будет жить мой ребёнок.
examples.trans: Yes, my child is going to live in my home.
Where's my toy car?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'life' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: У меня вопрос жизни и смерти.
examples.trans: I have a matter of life and death.

examples.text: Мама, перестань, не лезь в мою жизнь!
examples.trans: Mom, stop it, stay out of my life!

examples.text: Для начала наведи порядок в своей жизни.
examples.trans: First put your own life in order.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: This is my present for her.

examples.text: Ты хоть кроватку для ребёнка собрал?
examples.trans: Have you even assembled the crib for the baby?
I see, so you are doing this for a girl.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'чало'). Common neuter noun meaning 'beginning' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Для начала наведи порядок в своей жизни.
examples.trans: First put your own life in order.
It's only the beginning.
At the beginning of the week.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'вести'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to establish, bring', paired with 'наводить'.

examples.trans: I will establish iron order here.

examples.text: Дежурный офицер навёл идеальный порядок в части.
examples.trans: The duty officer established ideal order in the unit.

examples.text: Да, я наведу здесь железный порядок.
examples.trans: Yes, I will establish iron order here.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'рядок'). Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common masculine noun meaning 'order' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Для начала наведи порядок в своей жизни.
examples.trans: First put your own life in order.
Now let's go through everything in order.
Everything is in complete order.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'your, one's own', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You can quietly glue your crib back together.

examples.text: Нет, я свободна и очень рада.
examples.trans: No, I am single and very glad.

examples.text: Для начала наведи порядок в своей жизни.
examples.trans: First put your own life in order.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, it (is)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: After all, this is real theft.
Now what Senya does—that is theft.
Taste for yourself how delicious it is.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Ainura, we really should not do this.
After all, this is real theft.
Understand, these pastries will spoil by morning.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'звать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'invited', paired with 'звать'.

examples.text: Катя, подожди, это я его позвал.
examples.trans: Katya, wait, I was the one who invited him.

examples.text: Дядя Аркадий всё починит и позовёт.
examples.trans: Uncle Arkady will fix everything and call you.
To call a doctor.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'want', paired with 'захотеть'.

examples.text: Постараюсь прийти, ты ещё что-то хотел?
examples.trans: I will try to come, did you want something else?

examples.text: Я хотел вечером с тобой поговорить наедине.
examples.trans: I wanted to talk with you alone this evening.

examples.text: Я давно уже хотел тебе сказать.
examples.trans: I have wanted to tell you for a long time.

meanings.en: to be, to spend a little time
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'быть'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to be (for a while)', paired with 'быть'.

examples.text: Я хочу побыть сейчас совсем одна.
examples.trans: I want to be completely alone right now.
I want to be alone.
Let's stay here a little longer.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ейчас').

examples.trans: She is over there all alone right now.

examples.text: Мне бы сейчас получить деньги вперёд.
examples.trans: I would like to get the money up front right now.

examples.trans: Ainura, we really should not do this.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian cardinal or ordinal numeral meaning 'one', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Ну хорошо, тогда заходи к нам.
examples.trans: Well alright, come on in then.

examples.text: Налей мне водички на кухне, пожалуйста.
examples.trans: Pour me some water in the kitchen, please.
